title: Math 230 Final Project
text: During the second semester of my first year at Bucknell, I took a math class called Data Visualization and Computing. This class was my first introduction to R, and I learned a lot about the language and how to use it to construct helpful visualizations. The class culminated with a final project: a website that acted in part as a portfolio, housing the work that we had done throughout the year. The other aspect of the project was more open-ended, allowing us to build visualizations on a topic of our choice. I chose to examine the 2021 MLB season, and I crafted visualizations analyzing pitcher performance during that year. Use the link here to take a look.

title: The Evolution of the Major League Baseball Contract
text:
In the summer of 2023, I was fortunate enough to be accepted into a research program hosted by Bucknell University’s Library and Information Technology Department. The program, called the Digital Scholarship Summer Research Fellowship (DSSRF), aims to introduce students to digital tools and methodologies and then have them apply those skills to a research project of their choosing. Our cohort met nearly every day, first to learn these new digital tools and then to support each other as we worked through our research.
My research centered around the evolution of the Major League Baseball contract. I wanted to look at not only how the contracts themselves have changed, but also how the metrics that MLB teams value have changed. I split my work into three parts:

An interactive timeline that highlighted many of the sport’s important contractual developments, from professional baseball’s first contract in 1870 to Shohei Ohtani’s mammoth deal in the 2023 offseason.
Visualizations of data surrounding MLB free agent contracts for the purpose of highlighting trends and important variables.
A predictive model that aims to calculate what a certain player might receive in free agency.

Click on the attached link to see the full results of my research.

title: NHL Regression Modeling
text:
In the fall of 2024, I took a sports analytics class at Bucknell. For the final project, my group and I examined NHL data from recent seasons. We performed two types of regression on the data with the objective of predicting goals scored. We used R to generate a linear regression model and a Poisson regression model, using LASSO as a variable selection technique. We were able to determine which metrics had a significant association with goals scored. Additionally, we compared the models by mean absolute error (MAE) and adjusted \(R^2\). These model evaluation metrics indicated that the linear LASSO regression model was slightly more effective.
From there, we wanted to transfer goals scored into wins. In other words, we sought to answer the question, “How many additional goals must a team score in order to improve its record by one win?”. To do so, we employed the principles from the Pythagorean Theorem of Baseball and put them towards hockey. We found that, assuming goals allowed is held constant, 4.8 goals scored is worth one win. And from our regression analysis earlier, we were able to express wins in terms of the variable deemed significant in the linear model. For more detail, see the links provided.

title: About Me
text:
Since beginning at Bucknell University in the fall of 2021, I have participated in many activities both on and off-campus. At school, I have ran study groups, graded for math classes, and done research with professors. Outside the classroom, I have played club sports and mentored students acclimating to college. In the spring of 2024, I studied abroad in Athens, picking up not only a minor in Classics but also new experiences that have shaped my perspective of the world. Over the past two summers, I have been part of two research programs. In 2023, I was a fellow in Bucknell’s Digital Scholarship Summer Research Fellowship (DSSRF). The following year, I participated in the Carnegie Mellon Sports Analytics Camp (CMSACamp). Both summers, I worked on sports-specific projects that provided me with invaluable experience in the sports analytics world. See the “Projects” tab for results from that research and more.
I am a passionate sports fan, and one of the reasons I find statistics so interesting is because of how it overlaps with sports. When I have had the chance to choose topics for open-ended research, I often opt to explore sports-related questions, such as searching for a correlation between player statistics and MLB contracts or trying to model the time it takes to score the first points in an NFL game.

title: Weapons of Best Production: Predicting the Optimal Pitch Arsenal Adjustment for Superior Stuff+
text:
This summer, I had the amazing privilege of being part of the Carnegie Mellon Sports Analytics Camp, or CMSACamp for short. The program, hosted by CMU’s Department of Statistics and Data Science, focused on honing skills in statistical and data science methodology and applying those skills to the world of Sports Analytics. Our cohort, which was comprised of fifteen students in total, got to learn from exemplary faculty and instructors and hear from guest speakers who are experts in their respective fields.
The program culminated in a capstone project, with each group of three students worked with an advisor to solve a relevant problem in the world of sports. My groupmates, Gabriel Eze and Neha Kotha, and I worked with Samuel Fleischer, a Senior Quantitative Analyst for the Los Angeles Dodgers of Major League Baseball, and we were tasked with creating a pitch recommendation system that suggests, with conviction, the best pitch for an MLB pitcher to add to their arsenal. My group and I presented our work at the annual Carnegie Mellon Sports Analytics Conference in November. Check out the links on this page to see the results of our research.

title: NIST Uncertainty Machine
text: This summer, I worked with Bucknell Professor Sara Stoudt to create an updated version of the National Institute of Science and Technology (NIST) Uncertainty Machine. The original machine was created “to evaluate the measurement uncertainty associated with a scalar or vectorial output quantity that is a known and explicit function of a set of scalar input quantities for which estimates and evaluations of measurement uncertainty are available.” Prof. Stoudt and I were tasked with recreating the machine in R Shiny for more secure deployment and to take advantage of all that R Shiny has to offer. Our time frame was small, having only two weeks in August to work on the app before the start of the fall semester. However, we made great progress before turning it over to other app developers. The project was split into parts, and Prof. Stoudt and I were in charge of building a user interface that resembled the UI of the original website. The finished application is not ready yet, but it should be done soon. See the attached link to view the original NIST Uncertainty Machine and the format we were tasked with emulating.
